newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish court starts long road to EU judgement.
newsitem.headline: Danish court starts long road to EU judgement.

text.p: Government lawyers hope to resolve a legal challenge to Denmark's European Union membership quickly, but others said the case could take at least two years and would slow EU decision-making in the meantime.

The government, fighting a citizen's suit saying the terms of Denmark's EU membership contravened its constitution, wants the case kept simple and quick, with argument confined to the 1992 Maastricht treaty.

But the 11 petitioners, including a pensioner, a musician and a fish-seller, want to go back to the founding Treaty of Rome and call into evidence minutes of parliamentary committees dating back some 30 years.
They contend that, since Denmark joined in 1972, Brussels has taken over areas of national competence to an extent never envisaged in the original treaty.

"I hope that the problem about the documents is cleared up quickly and we can get to the important part of the matter," Laurids Mikaelsen, head of the Foreign Ministry legal department, said on Thursday.
A panel of three judges is to set the limits of the case on Friday and, although the hearing is a preliminary one, the rules that they lay down will have a significant bearing on the outcome.
Restricting the field of inquiry to 1992 and later will favour the government, while a more wide-ranging debate improves the odds for the challengers, lawyers say.
"We are very excited, because if the government lawyer loses on this our chance of success in the substantive trial is much better," said Christian Harlang, lawyer for the 11 petitioners.

The loser on Friday seems certain to appeal to the Supreme Court. After the rules are finally set, the main case will go to the district court, whose judgement will also be appealed as a matter of course.

European law professor Hjalte Rasmussen said a final verdict, in late 1998 at the earliest, was likely to be delivered by the Supreme Court's full plenum of 15 judges to give the fullest possible weight and integrity to the decision.
"If there has been any case in our history that merits full attention it is this one," he told Reuters.

The stakes are indeed high. A decision against the government, deemed by legal experts to be possible although perhaps not probable, would compel the government to return to the Euro drawing-board and renegotiate its EU membership.

Alternatively it could attempt the tortuous process of seeking to amend the constitution, by law requiring a general election and a referendum in which 40 percent of the entire electorate would have to approve its proposal.

At the very least, the uncertainty while a verdict is awaited is expected to hinder EU decision-making, notably the ratification next year of the results of the union's Inter governmental conference (IGC).
"How can you ratify the IGC before you are sure of the legality of what you are supposed to be ratifying," a diplomat said.

Denmark's threat to veto a joint European response to U.S. anti-Cuban trade laws, averted on Monday by a compromise after intense negotiation, was seen as an example of how the case could disrupt EU business before it even reached court.
